_about: College batch 8: freshman year (COL_008, 019, 022, 024-033). Opens The Advisor's Warning (hid_the_grade), {parent} Loses His Job (both COL_031 flags), and The Coach's Office (online_incident, academic_shortcut).

scenarios.title: Walk-On Reality
scenarios.text: Scholarship players get meal cards, new cleats and a laptop. You get a locker and a parking ticket. In the weight room, a teammate jokes that walk-ons are practice dummies, and a few guys laugh.

choices.label: Laugh it off and outwork them
choices.result: You laugh with them, then stay forty minutes after every lift for the rest of the week. Nobody says it again, mostly because they're tired of watching you.

choices.label: Say it back, calmly
choices.result: You tell him you're paying to be here, so you're probably the one who wants it most. The room goes quiet, then someone says, 'Fair.'

choices.label: Ask {coach} about a scholarship path
choices.result: After the lift you ask {coach}, plainly, what a walk-on has to do to earn a scholarship. The answer is long and honest, and you write it down.

scenarios.title: Homecoming Weekend
scenarios.text: Homecoming weekend. Alumni pack the campus, boosters want photos, the band wants the specialists for a halftime skit at Friday's pep rally, and the team wants you in bed by ten.

choices.label: Do the skit
choices.result: You learn the dance in an hour and do it in front of five thousand people. It's ridiculous, the clip goes around campus, and the band adopts you.

choices.label: Do the booster photos
choices.result: You spend an hour smiling for alumni photos. One of them owns the business you've wanted to intern at, and he gives you his card.

choices.label: Skip it all and rest
choices.result: You eat, stretch and are asleep by nine while the campus loses its mind outside your window.

scenarios.title: Budget Week
scenarios.text: Midterms, and your account is nearly empty. Rent, books and the phone bill are all due the same week, and you've been eating cereal for dinner since Sunday.

choices.label: Call {parent}
choices.result: You call {parent} and ask for help. He doesn't hesitate, and you hear how tight things are at home in the way he says 'it's fine.'

choices.label: Pick up a weekend shift
choices.result: You find a Saturday-morning shift at the campus bookstore. It eats your one free morning, and it covers the phone bill.

choices.label: Make a real budget
choices.result: You sit down with the team's financial-literacy person and build a budget for the rest of the semester. It's not fun. It works.

choices.label: Use the savings
choices.result: You dip into the savings you started with your first paycheck in high school. It covers the week, and you start a new rule: never below a hundred dollars.

scenarios.title: The New Holder
scenarios.text: Your new holder, {holder}, spins the laces toward the goalposts a different way than you're used to. You've each done it your own way for years, and neither of you wants to be the one to change.

choices.label: Change to {holder}'s way
choices.result: You adjust your approach to the new laces. The first week is ugly in practice, and by the second, you've stopped noticing.

choices.label: Ask {holder} to change
choices.result: You explain why the laces matter to your contact and ask {holder} to switch. It's done, a little stiffly.

choices.label: Chart both ways
choices.result: You suggest fifty reps each way, charted, and let the numbers decide. It costs a week of practice, and nobody has to win the argument.

choices.label: Tell {holder} what trust looks like
choices.result: You tell {holder} about the high school holder who never let you down and what that trust looked like. Then you ask what {holder} needs from you. You figure out the laces together by Friday.
choices.lock_text: having trusted a holder in a big moment before

scenarios.title: Sleepless Before Saturday
scenarios.text: You haven't slept more than four hours before a game all season. You lie awake at 2 a.m. replaying kicks you haven't even tried yet.

choices.label: Tell the team trainer
choices.result: You tell the trainer, who doesn't laugh. You leave with a sleep routine, a no-screens rule and the number for the team's sports psychologist.

choices.label: Watch film until you're tired
choices.result: You watch special teams film until your eyes close. You sleep a little more and dream about protection schemes.

choices.label: Just push through
choices.result: You decide it's part of the job and stop thinking about it. Some nights that works. Most nights it doesn't, so you fill them with extra film.

scenarios.title: The Class You're Failing
scenarios.text: A D on your chemistry midterm. {teacher} sees every athlete's grades on Friday, whether you mention it or not.

choices.label: Hope it gets lost
choices.result: You don't mention it and hope it slips through. It doesn't, and when {teacher} brings it up, it's the hiding that makes the conversation hard.

choices.label: Tell {teacher} first
choices.result: You walk into the office Thursday with the test in your hand. By the end of the meeting you have a tutor, a study table time and a plan.

choices.label: Fix it yourself
choices.result: You go to the professor's office hours twice a week and redo every problem you missed. You don't tell anyone, and the final goes better than anyone expected.

scenarios.title: Group Project Ghost
scenarios.text: A teammate in your class wants his name on your group project. He hasn't come to a single meeting, and the other two in your group are looking at you to decide.

choices.label: Leave his name off
choices.result: You tell the group his name stays off unless he does a section. He's cold to you at practice for a week.

choices.label: Give him one real job
choices.result: You give him the slides and a deadline. He does them, badly, at 2 a.m., and he shows up to the next meeting.

choices.label: Put his name on it
choices.result: You add his name and do his part yourself. It's easier than the argument, the project gets an A, and the rest of your group notices.

choices.label: Remember how covering went last time
choices.result: You covered for a teammate once in high school and remember how that went. You tell him plainly: show up Thursday, or his name stays off. He shows up, and you spend Thursday night catching him up.
choices.lock_text: having covered for a teammate before

scenarios.title: The Captain's Talk
scenarios.text: The senior captain pulls you aside after practice: some of the guys think you act like you're too good for the team. Specialists eat together, stretch together and leave together.

choices.label: Eat with the linemen
choices.result: For the next two weeks you sit at a different table every lunch. The linemen adopt you first; they say kickers are 'basically mascots,' affectionately.

choices.label: Ask what he means
choices.result: You ask the captain for specifics instead of guessing. It turns out to be one thing, leaving lifts early, and you fix it the next day.

choices.label: Keep your routine
choices.result: You say your routine is what makes you good and keep it. The captain shrugs, and the comments don't stop.

scenarios.title: The Highlight Clip
scenarios.text: A trick-shot clip of you from practice, the ball off the crossbar and into a trash can, goes around campus. Suddenly people you've never met want a picture.

choices.label: Make a few more
choices.result: You film a series of trick shots with the specialists on Sunday afternoons. The account grows, and so does the time it takes.

choices.label: Enjoy it and move on
choices.result: You take the pictures, thank people and don't film another one. It fades in a week, the way these things do.

choices.label: Ask {coach} what's okay to post
choices.result: You ask {coach} where the line is. The coach likes the question and sends you the team's social media guide.

scenarios.title: The Online Comment
scenarios.text: A fan account tears into you on Sunday: your form, your scholarship, your family. Your thumb is already on the reply button.

choices.label: Reply with exactly what you think
choices.result: You write it, send it and feel great for about ten minutes. By morning the screenshot is everywhere, and the athletic department's social media office wants a word.

choices.label: Put the phone down
choices.result: You put the phone in a drawer and go for a walk. It still stings the next day. It doesn't follow you anywhere.

choices.label: Mute the account and tell the staff
choices.result: You mute the account and send a screenshot to the team's media staff. They handle the part about your family; you never see it again.

choices.label: Do what worked before
choices.result: You dealt with something like this in high school, so you don't reply. You write the reply in your notes app, read it twice and delete it.
choices.lock_text: having handled an old post the right way before

scenarios.title: {parent}'s Phone Call
scenarios.text: {parent} sounds tired on the phone. His hours got cut at work, he says, but it's nothing for you to worry about.

choices.label: Offer to help
choices.result: You say you could pick up a job, send money, anything. He says no, firmly. He also says it means a lot that you asked.

choices.label: Take him at his word
choices.result: You say okay and turn the conversation to your week. He sounds relieved to talk about something else, and you keep your mind on school and football.

choices.label: Ask the real numbers
choices.result: You've helped at home before, so you ask how short the month is. He tells you, finally. You send what you can and agree to talk every Sunday.
choices.lock_text: having helped your family with money before

scenarios.title: The Sibling Visit
scenarios.text: {sibling} comes to campus for a weekend and wants to see everything: the locker room, the dorm and the parties he's heard about from his friends.

choices.label: Give him the real tour
choices.result: You show him the locker room, the film room and the dining hall at midnight, then watch a movie in your dorm. He says it's the best weekend of his year.

choices.label: Take him to the team barbecue
choices.result: You bring him to the team's Saturday barbecue, where linemen teach him to throw a spiral. It's loud and safe, and he talks about it for months.

choices.label: Say no to the parties, and why
choices.result: You tell him there's no party tour and explain why, without a lecture. He sulks for an hour, then asks if you can play video games instead.

scenarios.title: The Upperclassman's Notes
scenarios.text: An upperclassman offers you a copy of this semester's chemistry midterm, the real one, before the professor gives it. 'Everybody uses them,' he says.

choices.label: Take the folder
choices.result: You accept the folder. You score an A on the midterm, and a month later the professor changes the final, catches the pattern in the answers and reports half the class.

choices.label: Say no and study
choices.result: You say no thanks and spend Thursday night with the practice problems. You get a C-plus, and it's yours.

choices.label: Tell {teacher}
choices.result: You don't name him, but you tell {teacher} the midterm is out there. The professor writes a new exam, and nobody ever knows it was you.
